claim: Signal timing adaptation occurs through a network-wide resonance mechanism where intersections adjust their timing parameters to match the dominant traffic flow frequencies in the network.
mechanism: Each intersection continuously measures traffic flow patterns and identifies dominant frequencies (periodic patterns) in the arriving traffic. The intersection then adjusts its signal timing parameters to resonate with these dominant frequencies, similar to how slime mold conduits adapt their thickness to match flow frequencies in the organism.
evidence: Slime molds adapt conduit thickness to match flow frequencies
Traffic flow often exhibits periodic patterns
Resonance can optimize system performance in dynamic environments
assumptions: Traffic flow exhibits periodic patterns that can be identified locally
Resonance with flow frequencies leads to optimal timing
Intersections can identify and respond to dominant flow frequencies
expected_failure_modes: Inability to handle multiple conflicting frequencies
Sensitivity to noise in frequency detection
Failure to adapt to non-periodic traffic patterns
novelty_rationale: This hypothesis introduces a frequency-based adaptation mechanism rather than a queue-length or flow-based mechanism, focusing on temporal patterns rather than spatial distributions.
testability: The hypothesis can be tested by implementing a system where intersections identify dominant traffic flow frequencies and adjust timing parameters to resonate with these frequencies.
falsifier: If implementing frequency-based signal timing adjustment fails to improve network performance or creates timing conflicts when multiple dominant frequencies exist in different parts of the network, the hypothesis would be falsified.
